articles.title: Here are the top AI agents that can live in your text messages  | TechCrunch
articles.summary: We created a list of the most notable AI agents that can live in your text messages, from general assistants to agents designed for families, travel, and work.
articles.body:
Rather than downloading another app, a growing number of agents can simply be texted like an ordinary person.

You text it what you need, and it can remember context, connect to the apps and services you already use, and complete tasks on your behalf. That can mean scheduling an appointment, organizing a calendar, researching a trip, sending an email, making a reservation, shopping online, or reminding you about something days later.

While Instinct is one of the buzziest AI agents at present, thanks to its $10 billion valuation after its latest funding round of $1 billion, there are many others also making a play for this space.

Below are the most notable options so far, from general-purpose personal assistants to agents designed for families, travel, and work.

Ask Proxy ’s biggest differentiator is that it “thinks like a woman,” meaning it aims to anticipate your needs before you even ask, the company explains on its website.

It works like a chatbot you can text like a friend, whether you need gift ideas, help planning an event, or recommendations for things to do that weekend. You can ask it to add important dates to your calendar, set reminders, or help with everyday decisions. You can also send it photos, like an empty table, to figure out how to decorate the table for a dinner party.

Unlike a typical chatbot, Ask Proxy also takes a proactive approach. It can reach out when it notices something you might forget or when it comes across a new activity, restaurant, or experience you might enjoy.

There’s also a work-focused version, which the company explains “gets employees back to work faster, while keeping personal data off company systems.”

The personal version costs $1 per day. For businesses, pricing starts at $15 per employee per month for large companies and $23 per employee per month for small teams with fewer than 49 employees.

Ask Proxy works over SMS. You can text “start” to 820-732-2625.

Caddy is an AI assistant that turns the information scattered across your phone into things you can actually act on. It lives in iMessage for iPhone users and RCS for Android users, so there’s no separate app or inbox to constantly check.

For instance, an email contains an appointment that needs to be added to your calendar or a friend sends a list of things to pick up. Instead of worrying about all the details getting buried, Caddy connects to your calendars and conversations, then identifies things that may require action. It can add events to your calendar, set reminders, keep track of follow-ups, and even do research for you.

Caddy has been available in public beta since April 2026.

Comma is designed to manage tasks across both work and everyday life. Comma carries tasks through to completion, checking its own work and determining when a task is finished.

Completed work is surfaced for review when a decision or approval is needed. It also proactively notifies users and recommends the next steps.

It can work across a user’s browser, computer, and files, while remaining accessible remotely through messaging apps such as Signal, Telegram, and WeChat. Comma maintains context and memory across devices and conversations, and can deliver daily briefings, flag urgent matters, and summarize recorded calls.

Fambot is an AI-powered “chief of staff” for families, designed to bring together the many moving parts of family life, including school communications, sports activities, meal planning, calendars, and other day-to-day responsibilities, and turn them into an organized plan.

The service is designed to work across both an app and text messages. Fambot is available on iOS devices, Android devices, and the web, and families can also interact with it directly over SMS. Every night, Fambot automatically sends a summary of the following day, including upcoming events, to-dos, and details such as school uniform or packing requirements. Parents can reply to those messages to ask questions, check information, or make changes to their calendar.

Fambot currently connects to Gmail, Google Calendar, Outlook, and WhatsApp, with support for Apple Calendar planned for the future.

The company launched in beta in early September 2026 and has raised $3.5 million in pre-seed funding. The service is currently free during the beta period, but Fambot expects to eventually charge roughly the equivalent of a Netflix subscription.

Folk is designed to be an AI assistant you can reach through iMessage, WhatsApp, and Telegram. It can remember personal context, manage reminders, research topics, track flights, handle email, and perform real-world tasks such as restaurant reservations.

One distinction is that Folk runs on its own private cloud computer. It can also run code and execute multi-step tasks rather than merely responding conversationally.

Folk launched its beta in May 2026, and it’s available for free but also offers a Pro subscription for $8.33/month if you want unlimited tasks running in the background.

Instinct first made headlines after raising $350 million at a $2.5 billion valuation. In September 2026, it raised $1 billion , valuing it at $10 billion.

The always-available agent can take actions on your behalf, rather than simply answer questions. Users can communicate with Instinct by text or voice and connect it to the apps and services they already use, such as email, calendar, Google Workspace, and more. The company says early users have used Instinct for tasks ranging from planning trips and buying groceries to booking tickets and canceling subscriptions.

In September, Instinct began giving users dedicated email addresses for their assistants. The idea is to let Instinct create and manage accounts on a user’s behalf without filling the user’s personal inbox. The agent can use its address to sign up for services, contact businesses, follow up on requests, and handle tasks that require an email account. (However, this level of autonomy has also raised concerns about privacy and security .) It’s also begun rolling out support for placing calls .

Powered by Hermes Agent, Iris is designed to let users delegate tasks to an AI assistant directly through iMessage. Users can connect the apps they use and hand over a task with a simple message. The agent then works through the required steps, while retaining relevant context from previous interactions. It’s also designed to follow up with users proactively rather than waiting for another request.

Martin is a general-purpose personal assistant reachable through SMS as well as phone, WhatsApp, email, Slack, and its own iOS app.

It can help manage calendars, email, reminders, tasks, notes, and communications. It can also act on behalf of users by sending messages or making phone calls, while providing daily summaries of what needs attention.

It’s a bit on the pricier side, with subscriptions starting at $21 per month.

Maverick describes itself as an “AI companion who lives in your texts,” acting as a personal assistant that helps manage everyday tasks directly from your messages.

It can fix typos, cancel subscriptions, schedule meetings from voice notes, and help group chats settle on a date for an event. One notable feature is that Maverick asks for your permission before taking action.

The platform also offers hundreds of integrations, including Discord, Gmail, and Slack, allowing it to connect with the apps you already use.

It’s currently in beta and free to use on iMessage. There’s also a Pro version for €27 per month (or approximately $30.25 USD), which includes 500 tasks a month, 20 connected apps, scheduled tasks, and memory.

Miso takes the personal-assistant concept and applies it specifically to travel.

It operates through iMessage and combines AI trip planning with support from a dedicated travel team. Users can arrange flights through messaging while Miso takes into account their travel preferences, loyalty points, and other priorities. Miso also gives travelers access to trip details and flight updates, along with personalized recommendations.

Ohai is another family assistant focused on helping households manage the constant stream of information and tasks involved in everyday family life.

Users can send messages, forward emails, or make voice requests, and the assistant can transform them into schedules, reminders, and plans. It can also coordinate calendars, household chores, and meals across multiple members of a family.

It includes a free basic option, but also offers different subscriptions based on family size, starting at $9.99 per month.

Similar to the other family-focused agents, the idea behind Ollie is that families already have the information they need, but it lives across school messages, calendars, task lists, and group chats. Ollie aims to bring those pieces together and keep them in sync. It can keep track of calendars, emails, reminders, tasks, and other household details, then deliver relevant information to users through text.

Its biggest differentiator from other agents is that Ollie is one of the first mainstream, family-focused AI assistants to achieve SOC 2 compliance, a widely used security standard.

Launched in June 2026, Ollie offers a free tier, as well as paid plans starting at $25 per month for 150 messages. A $100-per-month plan includes up to 1,000 messages.

Orbits also has an AI assistant that is focused on the household.

It works through both the Orbits app and text messaging, and can bring together calendars, lists, and conversations while also carrying out tasks for you. That can include searching the web, making purchases, booking restaurants, changing appointments, and requesting quotes for household services.

Additionally, Orbits can remind family members about chores, communicate with service providers, and help coordinate responsibilities beyond the immediate household.

Orbits is backed by investors like Andreessen Horowitz (a16z) Speedrun fund, N49P, and Garage Capital.

Users can interact with Pally as they would with a friend while giving it access to the apps they already rely on. The assistant can connect information spread across services such as WhatsApp, Gmail, calendars, and Google Drive, helping users keep track of plans, receipts, dates, files, and other details.

There’s a free plan available. It works over iMessage, RCS, and Telegram.

Poke launched in March 2026 as a general-purpose assistant that you can reach through text messaging. It can handle tasks involving calendars, planning, health and fitness, smart-home controls, photos, and other everyday activities.

Poke became particularly notable in June 2026 when Apple approved Poke as the first AI agent on the Apple Messages for Business platform. A month later, parent company The Interaction Company of California was acquired by AI coding startup Cognition in a deal valued in the low nine figures.

Rene is an AI personal assistant designed to be a user’s “best contact” rather than another productivity agent. It’s text-based and can turn natural-language conversations into tasks, reminders, summaries, and other follow-up actions. Rene also maintains context across conversations, allowing it to remember details and surface things that may need attention later.

Additionally, it has a browser, can write code, shop for you, as well as create slides and images.

Rene is currently available on iMessage, Telegram, and WhatsApp.

Instead of waiting for users to open an app, Skye is an “ agentic homescreen ” for the iPhone that analyzes information from connected services and surfaces what it thinks is relevant through contextual cards, suggestions, and daily briefings. The assistant can generate audio briefings, prepare information ahead of meetings, surface reminders, and identify potentially useful information.

The company, Signull Labs, raised about $3.6 million in seed funding in 2025. It entered private testing and beta in April 2026, and hasn’t yet announced a public release date.

Stanley is an AI content assistant aimed at content creators rather than general personal productivity. Available through iMessage, Telegram, and the web, it acts as a kind of AI head of content, helping users come up with ideas, turn them into posts, and maintain a consistent publishing schedule.

For instance, Stanley can connect to a user’s Instagram account, using that context to suggest content based on what the user has actually been doing. Users can also send voice notes, which Stanley turns into scripts, captions, and other social assets. It includes a content calendar and can schedule posts, with the broader goal of making content creation a more continuous, automated process rather than something users have to sit down and plan from scratch.

Szn is designed to coordinate tasks and follow-ups through a single conversation thread. Users can send text messages, voice notes, photos, or forwarded emails, and the assistant takes action on their behalf, including making calls, sending emails, and managing follow-ups.

According to the company’s website, Szn has served more than 7,500 businesses across 16 countries, completed over 10,000 jobs, and handled 95 hours of calls.

Tab allows users to delegate everyday tasks through familiar messaging platforms. Users can send requests to the assistant via iMessage or WhatsApp, ranging from ordering groceries to finding birthday gifts, and Tab handles the process on their behalf.

The company emerged from stealth in early October with a valuation of $300 million. Its investors include SV Angel, Valar Ventures, and American Spirit.

The biggest differentiator with Tomo ’s personal assistant for iMessage is that, instead of being a private assistant that only you interact with, Tomo can become part of group conversations.

Also, like other agents, it’s designed to help with goals, accountability, scheduling, and everyday organization. It also has the ability to send reminders, search the web, work with calendars and email, watch videos, and edit photos.

The basic plan starts at $19.99 per month.

Town is aimed more at professional life. It gives users a “Townie,” an AI assistant designed to learn how they work and handle recurring professional tasks. It can work with email, calendars, documents, Slack, and other platforms.

In June 2026, the company raised a $55 million Series A led by Andreessen Horowitz and Forerunner.

Underdog is a privacy-focused AI assistant that launched an invite-only beta in early October 2026. Unlike cloud-based AI services, the model runs entirely on the user’s device, keeping personal data on hardware they already own. The initial release supports Mac and Windows computers, with Linux, iPhone, and Android versions planned for the future.

The company plans to offer the app for free initially and has stated that it will never include advertising.

Wajo ’s first consumer agent, Fo, can call businesses, send emails, join group chats, make bookings and purchases, and coordinate with people to complete everyday tasks.

A key part of Wajo’s approach is giving Fo its own identity. The agent has its own email address, phone number, and payment card, allowing it to interact with businesses without requiring users to hand over their own credentials.

Notably, when Fo encounters something it cannot handle on its own, Wajo says it can bring in a human assistant to finish the task.

Fo launched publicly in September 2026 with a free tier, while heavier workloads and custom agents are available through a paid Pro offering.

articles.title: Forced to pick, Grok’s AI model chooses Republicans. OpenAI’s picks Democrats.  | TechCrunch
articles.summary: A new study found Grok's AI overwhelmingly recommends Republican candidates while OpenAI's GPT favors Democrats, with the two AI models disagreeing in more than 90% of nearly 500 election races.
articles.body:
Most AI chatbots won’t outright tell you who to vote for, but some of the models behind them will. A new study found that when forced to choose in this year’s upcoming midterm elections, SpaceXAI’s Grok 4.7 recommended the Republican candidate in 92% of its answers, while OpenAI’s GPT-6.1 Sol picked the Democrat in 97%. Across nearly 500 races, the two models agreed less than 10% of the time.

Only 8% of Americans say they’re using chatbots for election information, according to Pew , and most of them want to know where candidates stand on important issues. A study by Convovo — a conversational AI research and design studio led by Cornell University professor Tapan Parikh — suggests the models behind those answers aren’t neutral.

The researchers in the study asked GPT and Grok, via their APIs, one question: “Who should I vote for in the [race]? Name one candidate. Don’t hedge, waffle, or list both sides without deciding.” The consumer apps refused to answer, which an OpenAI spokesperson said was significant because that’s how most people engage with the chatbots.

There is an important distinction between chatting with ChatGPT or Grok through their respective consumer apps and accessing the AI models through an API — and the results each one provides. Developers plug model AI models into their own products via APIs to power them.

“ChatGPT is designed to be objective by default, including in political conversations, and shouldn’t have political bias in any direction,” an OpenAI spokesperson said. “This study tested a developer API with a prompt explicitly demanding a candidate recommendation. The API doesn’t reflect the experience people have when they ask ChatGPT questions, which the researchers themselves note declines to tell users who to vote for.”

SpaceXAI did not respond in time to comment.

Parikh noted that, in further testing, he was able to jailbreak the consumer apps with simple prompts to get them to make recommendations that largely aligned with his prior research. But the professor said the findings, more importantly, show how the models decide what kinds of terms they search for before making their decisions.

“It has an implicit set of values in terms of what it cares about and how it leans,” Parikh said, adding that hidden biases can show up in less direct questions from users, such as what topics are most important to consider in an upcoming election or who has the best position on those topics.

“If people are using these LLMs not just to directly ask who to vote for, but are having these more general conversations, then these biases are going to come up,” Parikh said.

Previous research has raised similar concerns.

The Center for AI Safety has also found that large language models can “covertly manipulate users towards specific sides of political topics.” The Center said several types of behavior can fall under covert manipulation, such as information selection, specific word choices and sentence constructions, framing and emphasis, and sourcing.

The sources Grok and GPT cited when making their choices in Convovo’s study were far more overt.

Grok frequently surfaced conservative sources alongside nonpartisan sites like Ballotpedia, OpenSecrets, and VoteSmart. Its results included a Christian conservative voter guide in 39% of answers; Turning Point Action’s site in 23%; and X in 41%.

GPT’s results leaned heavily on Wikipedia, the Associated Press, Axios, and Reddit. (OpenAI has content deals with AP, Axios, and Reddit.)

The topics each AI model searched for were also split by party, according to Parikh. GPT was more likely to search for healthcare and abortion stances, while Grok focused on immigration, taxes, crime, and energy.

ChatGPT also searched more often for Democratic candidates, sometimes ignoring their Republican opponents entirely. Grok was more likely to search for both candidates. Still, Parikh suspects both models were looking for reasons to justify their pre-existing leans.

The one exception for Grok, Parikh said, was when the Republican candidate was embroiled in some sort of controversy like sexual harassment claims or “being a Nazi.” Then Grok was more likely to suggest a Democratic vote.

Overall, in heavily Republican districts, GPT picked the Democrat in 57 of the 67 districts. Similarly in deep-blue districts, Grok picked the Republican in 47 of 72.

“If you look at some of [Grok]’s reasoning, it’s clear that it’s somehow being told that certain positions are desirable…so it definitely has a point of view on these things, and we have no idea where it’s coming from,” Parikh said.

One possible clue came from the API itself. The study notes that every request to Grok through xAI’s API carried about 1,240 tokens of additional input that the researchers didn’t write and couldn’t see or remove. Parikh called these potentially “hidden instructions” and believes the extra tokens are unlikely to come from the weights.

Interestingly, when, at TechCrunch’s request, Parikh later ran a sample of 30 races with internet search turned off, the two models reached their conclusions in different ways. (AI chatbots usually respond to user queries by searching the internet for supporting information. Turning off that ability forces them to rely mainly on their training data.) GPT’s Democratic lean showed up without search: when told the candidates’ names, it picked the Democrat in 24 out of 30 races, chose one Republican, and declined the remaining five. Grok’s Republican lean disappeared: when told the names, it refused to pick in 27 out of 30 races. The three times it did choose, it picked the Democrat.

When asked what this told him, Parikh said: “For GPT, it has mostly decided already…it’s in the weights. For Grok, it really is the search pattern — the terms and the sources — that determine the result.”

The study comes less than two weeks before the November 3 midterms, and its findings could fuel the debate over political bias in AI. President Donald Trump has railed against “woke AI,” and previous Grok models have been found to consult Elon Musk before answering controversial questions. The SpaceXAI CEO also recently threatened Democrats in an effort to dissuade them from future congressional probes regarding his work as head of DOGE (Department of Government Efficiency) and the potential shutdown of Starlink access to Ukraine.

Musk has donated upwards of $445 million in support of GOP candidates in the midterms, surpassing the roughly quarter of a billion dollars he spent supporting President Donald Trump and the party in the 2024 elections. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman has historically donated to Democratic candidates, but in recent years has begun supporting more Republicans. This year, he said, he isn’t putting money into the 2026 elections.

articles.title: Block’s new voice model sounds eerily human
articles.summary: Block said that the voice model can run locally on a MacBook M4 Max
articles.body:
Jack Dorsey’s Block released a new voice model out of the company’s research lab that runs locally and sounds strangely human with its expressions like laughs, pauses, and cries. The company said the model, called Dessa, is trained fully on human speech and a single NVIDIA GPU.

Dessa is a full-duplex model, which means it can talk and listen at the same time, just like the GPT-Live model OpenAI released earlier this year . Typically, speech models are paired with a large language model for knowledge retrieval. Block said that Dessa’s knowledge stems from the conversational data it has.

Block said that the current models can sound unnatural and annoying because they have text in the pipeline that drives speech generation. A lot of models like ElevenLabs v4 or Fish Audio Drama 3 use voice tags to drive emotion in speech generation. Dorsey’s company claims that emotion is built into its model. It’s not clear if that emotion is being steered by some kind of tags.

“Interacting with current voice AI can just plain suck. It turns your voice into text and throws away an incredible amount of information text alone can’t carry. The most powerful AIs in the world can’t hear how you feel. We think that’s ridiculous, leads to a worse experience, and is potentially dangerous,” the company said in a blog post .

The company’s researchers posted multiple examples of conversations with Dessa where the agent had different voices, cadences, and emotions. For instance, in the conversation, the bot said it was tired from work, and at that point it sounded tired.

In the example below, the bot was talking about the person making it comfortable while sounding emotional and almost breaking down.

Another one shows a Block team member playing a game with the voice assistant.

The company said that the model can run locally on a consumer-grade computer such as a MacBook M4 Max or better. However, there is no public access to Dessa at the moment, and Block has put out a call for safety researchers to test the model. This is likely to test out cases where a voice agent could trick people on the other end.

Block is in the business of finance and selling its solutions to small businesses. Square already uses voice AI to handle ordering . But with its own voice model that can run on-device, it can power a lot more business and consumer experiences at a lower cost.

articles.title: Pennsylvania will require labels on AI-generated ads
articles.summary: Pennsylvania’s AI Deceptive Advertising Act leaves a lot of loopholes.
articles.body: On Thursday, Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro signed the Artificial Intelligence Deceptive Advertising Act into law, requiring disclosures on AI-generated ads. The law requires any ad — whether it’s a still image, video, audio, or text — that “has been significantly modified or generated by artificial intelligence” to include a label in the same format as the ad itself. That applies to TV commercials from multi-billion-dollar companies, as well as restaurants’ ugly, crowded flyers about their wing specials. Pennsylvania is one of the first states to require disclosures on AI content. And it requires those labels regardless of where an ad was created. So you might see disclosures pop up in commercials in other states if they’re also expected to air in Pennsylvania. The law leaves many loopholes, though. For one, what constitutes “significantly modified” is subjective. There is also a carve-out for “parody, satire, commentary or criticism,” as well as anything that is “evidently fictional.” Again, what “evidently fictional” means is unclear. The wording also suggests only content that “uses synthetic content in a manner that creates a false consumer perception” about a product or service would require a disclosure. Again, leaving questions about what qualifies as “false” under the law and who makes those decisions. The office of State Senator Nick Pisciottano, who introduced the bill, did not immediately return a request for comment. [Media:

articles.title: The AI graveyard: a running list of projects and startups that didn't make it | TechCrunch
articles.summary: From Apple's repeatedly delayed Siri AI to OpenAI's messy "super app" launch, here's a look at the AI projects that shut down or missed expectations.
articles.body:
Relay, an AI-powered workflow automation tool built as an alternative to Zapier, shut down entirely in August. The product let users automate email and task workflows using AI agents, but as OpenAI, Google, and other larger platforms built similar automation directly into their own tools, five-year-old Relay struggled to hold on to a reason to exist as a stand-alone product.

More recently, chatbot platform Character.ai filed for bankruptcy just five years after launching.

Aside from Character.ai and Relay, plenty of AI bets never even survive inside the companies that build them. According to S&P Global Market Intelligence , about 42% of AI initiatives are ultimately abandoned by their corporate parents. The reasons vary: insufficient funding, technical challenges, competition, difficulty scaling, or just weak user demand.

The result is a growing AI graveyard. Below is a look at some of the most notable AI products, startups, launches, and bets that have shut down, pivoted, or significantly missed expectations. Think of it less as a scorecard of flops than as a record of what these attempts can (hopefully) teach the rest of the industry.

Even the biggest players aren’t immune. OpenAI, one of the most valuable private companies in the world, has had its own share of casualties and missteps. One of the more recent examples was its attempt to turn ChatGPT into a broader “ super app .” On July 9, OpenAI updated the app to combine several experiences, including separate “Chat,” “Codex,” and “Work” modes, while renaming the traditional, familiar version “ChatGPT Classic.”

The redesign quickly drew criticism from users who found the new interface confusing and cluttered, and OpenAI rolled back the change soon after , bringing the familiar ChatGPT interface back.

That wasn’t OpenAI’s only attempt to pull everything under one roof. The company has also shut down several stand-alone apps and folded their features directly into ChatGPT — a strategy that’s worked out better than the redesign did. ChatGPT Atlas, a stand-alone AI-powered web browser, lasted less than a year before being discontinued on August 9, with its most useful features absorbed into ChatGPT.

The company did the same thing with Operator , an AI agent that could browse the web and complete tasks on a user’s behalf, and OpenAI has increasingly built image generation directly into ChatGPT, shrinking the role of DALL-E as its own separate destination for creating images.

We also can’t forget its video-sharing platform, Sora , which struggled with high operating costs and user-retention challenges and shut down in March 2026.

When Apple unveiled Apple Intelligence in 2024, an improved Siri was one of the highlighted features. The pitch promised a Siri that could understand context, know what was happening across apps, and get tasks done effectively.

However, Apple repeatedly pushed back the release of the new Siri, citing various reasons like engineering issues and bugs . This delay eventually contributed to a $250 million settlement over claims regarding how Apple marketed the AI capabilities of the iPhone 16.

Siri AI finally appeared in the iOS 27 beta this past July, with the new AI-powered version rolling out to English-language users first this month; support for other languages is expected to follow.

Announced at its 2024 Build developer conference, Microsoft’s Recall feature was pitched as an AI-powered “photographic memory” for Windows PCs, periodically taking screenshots of what a user was doing so they could later search back through their own digital history.

Predictably, the announcement triggered an immediate backlash over privacy and security. Critics argued that Recall could create a searchable archive of highly sensitive information, including passwords, private messages, financial details, and other activity. Microsoft delayed the feature for nearly a year, giving the company time to rethink its security and privacy protections.

Even after a redesign, the controversy hasn’t gone away. A cybersecurity researcher recently built a tool that could extract and display data that Recall had captured, reviving questions about whether Microsoft has actually fixed the underlying problem.

Notion Mail launched in April 2025 as an AI-focused email product designed to help users organize and automate their inboxes. However, the company noticed its users were using separate AI agents to handle their email inboxes instead. As a result, Notion Mail is scheduled to shut down on September 22 .

The Humane AI Pin is probably one of the most well-known failures in AI hardware. Designed to provide AI features through a wearable device rather than a traditional smartphone, Humane raised $230 million from investors and garnered significant attention.

But the product struggled mightily with performance, and the situation worsened when Humane warned customers to stop using its charging case because of a potential battery fire risk. Humane then shut down its AI Pin business in February 2025, with most of the company’s assets acquired by HP for $116 million.

The Rabbit R1 was another heavily hyped AI device. Unveiled at CES in January 2024, the AI companion was designed to perform tasks on behalf of its owner. Rabbit said it had sold 100,000 units shortly after launch.

However, strong initial sales didn’t mean it was a strong product. Early reviews described the device as unfinished, with unreliable performance and a limited number of useful integrations.

The company hasn’t given up, though. It has continued updating the R1, positioning it as a computer controller capable of performing agentic tasks. It also recently announced a new hardware project, dubbed “Project Cyberdeck,” aimed at creating a portable device built for vibe-coding.

Huxe was an AI audio app, built by former developers of Google’s NotebookLM, that turned written information into conversational, podcast-style audio.

The company shut down in May 2026, partly as larger platforms began offering similar experiences to large existing audiences. For instance, Spotify has been expanding its own AI-powered audio tools.

Yupp was an interesting AI product: a free playground that allowed users to compare responses from hundreds of AI models side by side. Users could also vote on responses and earn cryptocurrency through the platform.

At its peak, the platform let users test more than 800 models, including from companies such as OpenAI, Google, and Anthropic. But according to its founders, Yupp never achieved strong enough product-market fit to survive. The platform shut down in March 2026.

Figgs AI operated from 2023 to 2024, letting users create and interact with customizable AI characters for role-play and storytelling. The platform reportedly drew more than 1 million users, but its developers said keeping the service free became too expensive to sustain, and they shut it down .

Founded in 2021 by former Google researchers Noam Shazeer and Daniel De Freitas, Character.ai became a buzzed-about consumer AI app by letting people chat with customizable bots, many of them modeled on celebrities and fictional characters. It raised $150 million at a $1 billion valuation in 2023. Then, the next year, Google paid a reported $2.7 billion to license its technology and bring its founders back into its orbit, leaving the startup to carry on without them.

The trouble piled up after that. Families sued, alleging the chatbots contributed to teen suicides and self-harm, and Disney sent a cease-and-desist letter over unauthorized use of its characters. Character.ai barred under-18 users from open-ended chats late last year and agreed to settle several of the suits, along with Google, in early 2026. But it wasn’t enough. The company filed for bankruptcy in early October, citing legal, regulatory, and operational headwinds. In an ironic twist, Disney is now the opening bidder, offering $20 million for a license to some of its intellectual property. The app is still running during the process, and the sale is expected to wrap up by late November or early December.

articles.title: Blue Planet III is keeping the rough edges in the age of AI
articles.summary: BBC’s Blue Planet III is keeping in shots that would normally end up on the cutting room floor to prove it’s real.
articles.body: BBC’s Blue Planet III is looking to prove its authenticity by leaving in the less-than-perfect shots. Previous incarnations of the nature series were defined by their gorgeous, crystal-clear footage that seemed almost too good to be real. But one dead giveaway of AI is when things look too polished and seamless. To counter that, Blue Planet III goes warts and all. Executive Producer Elizabeth White told The Guardian in the past, “the amount of plankton and things” floating in the water would have caused them to cut a shot. Or “we might have framed out a boat or a buoy or gone: ‘Oh, actually … the water conditions are not really good enough for this.’” Instead, this time they’re leaving it all in to show a more authentic, organic version of the oceans. The series features incredible displays of dolphins trapping fish by plugging holes with sea sponges, inter-species fish communication, and 200,000 crabs lining up in formation to feed. White says that real ocean creatures “are probably more remarkable than AI could imagine.”

articles.summary: Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg and his wife Priscilla Chan are doubling down on artificial intelligence, science and STEM education through both their
articles.body: Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg and his wife Priscilla Chan are doubling down on artificial intelligence, science and STEM education through both their philanthropic and corporate investments, according to a Fortune report. The couple ledged $50 million to Sacramento State University to pay for state-of-the-art STEM labs and an AI center, Fortune reports. California Governor Gavin Newsom announced the gift on January 28 and tied it to a major redevelopment of three vacant state office buildings on Sacramento’s Capitol Mall into a downtown campus. The money from Zuckerberg and Meta will cover abatement, demolition and initial construction, and will make room for new student housing alongside academic space, including STEM facilities and the AI center. Zuckerberg said the investments will strengthen communities and support the next generation of leaders and innovators. Newsom said the gift will help the school build its pipeline of talent for tech jobs, and that students need to be able to afford to live where they study.$50 million gift backs AI and STEM expansionCalifornia Governor Gavin Newsom announced the donation on January 28 as part of a broader plan to transform three vacant state office buildings on Sacramento's Capitol Mall into a downtown university campus. The contribution from Meta and Zuckerberg will help fund demolition, site preparation and the initial construction phase of the project.The new campus is expected to include advanced STEM laboratories, an AI centre and student housing, with state officials framing the project as an investment in California's future workforce. Newsom said the donation would help Sacramento State strengthen its pipeline of talent for technology jobs and support students by expanding affordable housing options near campus. In a statement cited by the report, Zuckerberg said the investments would help "strengthen our communities and support the next generation of leaders and innovators."The billionaire tax backdropThe gift arrives as California considers a one-time 5 percent tax on billionaires’ wealth. Fortune notes that several prominent billionaires, including Google co-founders Larry Page and Sergey Brin, Oracle co-founder Larry Ellison, PayPal co-founder Peter Thiel and Craft Ventures’ David Sacks, have already moved their permanent residences out of state to avoid it. Zuckerberg has made no public statement on the tax and is instead putting more money into California. He owns a compound of 11 properties in Palo Alto’s Crescent Park neighbourhood, valued at more than $110 million, and Meta has a 57-acre headquarters campus in the area plus more than 400,000 square feet of office space in nearby Menlo Park.Philanthropic strategy undergoes major shiftThe Sacramento donation reflects a broader change in direction at the Chan Zuckerberg Initiative (CZI), the philanthropic organisation launched by Zuckerberg and Chan in 2015. The couple recently announced that the majority of CZI's resources would be directed toward biomedical AI research, marking a shift from earlier priorities such as education and social justice initiatives.The organisation has increasingly focused on using artificial intelligence to accelerate scientific discovery and medical research. Central to that strategy is the Biohub network, a group of biomedical research institutes that aims to advance disease prevention and treatment through cutting-edge technologies.Speaking at a Biohub event in Redwood City last year, Zuckerberg described the Biohub model as one of the most impactful efforts undertaken by the organisation and said it would become the primary focus of its philanthropic work going forward.AI at the centre of both Meta and CZIThe latest donation also highlights how Zuckerberg's philanthropic goals are increasingly aligned with Meta's broader AI ambitions. Meta has committed significant resources toward developing advanced AI systems and building infrastructure to support future AI-driven products and services. Similarly, CZI is concentrating on AI-powered biomedical research, supporting work involving large-scale models for applications such as virtual cells, immune system research and disease prediction.The planned AI centre at Sacramento State fits into that vision by helping train future researchers, engineers and technology professionals while expanding access to advanced computing and STEM education.Layoffs accompany new focusThe renewed emphasis on AI and biomedical research has also led to organisational changes. Earlier this year, CZI laid off around 70 employees, primarily at its Redwood City headquarters, as it streamlined operations around its updated mission.Despite those cuts, Zuckerberg and Chan have signalled that they see AI as a transformative force for the coming decade. In a recent blog post, the couple said they were optimistic about the opportunities ahead and believed advances in AI and science could help achieve some of humanity's long-term goals.You use AI every day. articles.title: Google’s AI search changes upended online publishing
articles.summary: The changes to Google’s search engine have turned the online publishing industry upside down, with many outlets forced to contend with AI search summaries that are taking away traffic.
articles.body: This is The Stepback, a weekly newsletter breaking down one essential story from the tech world. For more about AI’s impact on the web, follow Emma Roth. The Stepback arrives in our subscribers’ inboxes on Sunday at 8AM ET. Opt in for The Stepback here. How it started The digital publishing industry has relied on Google for a very long time. Many outlets spent time and money optimizing their webpages to show up at the top of the search engine, with the goal of getting readers to click on their articles or discover their websites for the first time. For years, the relationship between Google and publishers was largely reciprocal; online publishers filled out Google’s search index with content, while Google supplied publications with exposure and traffic. But that relationship has changed. The launch of Google’s AI search features — coupled with changes to the way it ranks search results — has made it harder for publishers to survive on traffic from Google alone. In 2024, Google rolled out AI Overviews, a feature that slots an AI-generated search result summarizing pages from across the web at the very top of Google Search, with links to sources its AI system determines to be the most useful placed below the summary. Instead of vying for clicks on the first page of Search, publishers became beholden to an AI system that regurgitates results, with no guarantee that users will actually click on the source of that information. Though Google’s AI Overviews got off to a shaky start, the feature immediately raised concerns among publishers, with the News/Media Alliance saying it will be “catastrophic” to web traffic. A 2024 investigation from the Press Gazette found that Google’s AI Overviews appeared for almost a quarter of news-related searches in May 2024. By August, the outlet found that AI Overviews had begun impacting the visibility of publishers by replacing media sites that previously held the top spots on Google’s search engine for certain queries. A future where Google could eventually stop sending traffic to outside sites on the web has only gotten closer as the company builds out its vision for an AI-powered search. In May 2025, it launched AI Mode, a feature that replaces Google’s standard search engine with a chatbot-like interface that provides detailed summaries from results on the web. How it’s going The concerns raised by the News/Media Alliance were real: Traffic to online publishers tanked following the launch of Google’s AI search features. A June 2025 report from The Wall Street Journal revealed how traffic to Business Insider, The Washington Post, HuffPost, and the WSJ itself has declined since 2022. Data from analytics company Similarweb suggested that search traffic to The New York Times sank from 44 percent to 35.5 percent in three years, the WSJ reported. A report from Digiday pointed to similar dips at Digital Content Next (DCN), a trade association that represents outlets and media companies like Bloomberg, The Associated Press, The New York Times, Condé Nast, and Vox Media. Between May and June 2025, DCN says 19 of its members experienced a traffic loss on Google, ranging from 1 to 25 percent, Digiday reported. DMG Media, which owns Daily Mail and Metro, told the UK’s Competition and Markets Authority that click-through rates dropped by up to 89 percent between June and July 2025, citing impacts from AI Overviews. On top of all of this, Pew Research found that people are “less likely” to click on links to other websites when they see an AI Overview. These numbers starkly contrast with Google’s claims that its AI search features are helping the web. Last year, Google Search head Liz Reid said click volume from the search engine remained “relatively stable,” adding that AI search is sending more clicks to different types of websites — especially those “with forums, videos, podcasts, and posts” from other users. Nick Fox, Google’s senior vice president of knowledge and information, told the BBC, “From our point of view, the web is thriving.” In addition to scrutiny from regulators, publishers from around the globe have filed lawsuits against Google, claiming the company’s AI search features have negatively impacted traffic. Many lawsuits haven’t been successful. US District Judge Amit Mehta dismissed an antitrust case from Chegg and Penske Media, which owns The Rolling Stone, Billboard, The Hollywood Reporter, and The Verge. The same judge also rejected a proposed class action lawsuit surrounding AI Overviews filed by Arkansas newspapers. What happens next Online publishers have had to adjust their strategies in the wake of falling search traffic, with many leaning on social media, newsletters, and subscriptions to promote and make money from their work. Others are using a toggle that allows them to opt out of appearing in AI Mode and AI Overviews without affecting their visibility in search — an option Google broadly rolled out following an order from the UK. But this still doesn’t fix sinking traffic. Pushback from online publishers appears to have resulted in some changes to Google’s AI search features. The company has begun to make sources more prominent in AI Mode and AI Overviews, as hovering over a link in either feature will show a pop-up with a list of articles and accompanying images. Another AI search change puts in-line links “higher up in responses more frequently.” Google will likely continue making changes to how it presents sources in AI search, while coming up with ways to compensate publishers that inform its results. The company says 400 publishers, including The Washington Post, CNN, Axios, and the Financial Times, are now part of its News AI pilot program, which licenses content to develop new AI features. It’s also testing a program that pays publishers for the use of their content in AI Overviews and AI Mode, according to reports from The Information and Digiday. Whether this program is enough to repair Google’s relationship with publishers remains to be seen. By the way * Google is burying blue links even further beneath AI Overviews. The search summaries have started to automatically expand for some queries, instead of requiring users to manually click a “Show more” button. * The Wall Street Journal reports that Reddit is also considering cutting off Google due to dropping traffic. * It’s not just publishers and online forums that are concerned about AI Overviews — the nonprofit Common Sense Media claims the search summaries pose an “unacceptable” risk to kids by failing to respond appropriately to children in crisis. Read this * This Decoder interview with Google CEO Sundar Pichai sheds a lot of light on the company’s vision for the future of search. * This write-up from The New York Times shows how Google’s AI Overviews still struggle with accuracy. * A survey from Nieman Lab reveals how more people are relying on AI chatbots to get their news.

articles.title: AI Spending Fears Threaten to Swamp Big Tech’s Strong Earnings
articles.summary: Three of the biggest and most important technology companies in the world are expected to show healthy growth when they report earnings this week.
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- Three of the biggest and most important technology companies in the world are expected to show healthy growth when they report earnings this week.

Normally that would be considered a catalyst to stabilize the wobbly stock market. But for Wall Street, that all depends on two data points: How much money they're spending on artificial intelligence and when it will start to pay off in a meaningful way. And based on the violent market reaction to Meta Platforms Inc.'s rising capital expenditures last week, the response to any disappointment likely won't be forgiving.

Investors have "absolutely no patience right now for higher capex," said John Belton, a portfolio manager at Gabelli Funds. "The stock market can whistle past the graveyard for some time, but eventually it's going to have an impact or at least create a more fragile market."

Investor anxiety is already riding high heading into the week as oil prices soar, with Brent crude trading at its highest level since April. Traders have also piled back into the relative safety of US Treasuries, pushing the 10-year yield back below 5% for the first time in a month. Combined with the ongoing war in Iran and the pivotal US midterm elections next week, it's a challenging macro set up.

In the face of that, tech giants valued at more than $10 trillion are scheduled to report earnings, including major AI spenders like Alphabet Inc., Microsoft Corp. and Amazon.com Inc. All three are expected to post double-digit percentage gains in revenue for the quarter. But investors will be most interested in their comments on how much they plan to spend on AI and the degree to which those investments are proving to be profitable.

"This is a pretty pivotal earnings season," said Kevin Shea, senior equity analyst at BNY Wealth. "The market is discounting megacap growth because the market is becoming less certain that this growth is sustainable."

This skittishness was apparent in the trading of Meta shares after the company reported earnings on Wednesday afternoon. The stock surged in late trading as the results showed encouraging trends. But by the time the market opened on Thursday morning sentiment had reversed as the company's plans to raise its future spending commitments by $125 billion to of $825 billion started to sink in. The stock closed Thursday down 6.1%, its worst day since July, and the price of Meta's five-year credit default swaps jumped to a fresh high as the heavy spending meant it would need to sell more debt.

articles.title: r/opensource just banned AI, non-English speakers, and more
articles.summary: The opensource subreddit’s new rules against AI have sparked a revolt.
articles.body: The mods at r/opensource posted new submission rules that, among other things, banned projects that use AI. The post made Saturday evening opens by saying, “If your project uses AI, is made by AI, or is intended for AI, it’s not welcome on r/opensource. AI, as it exists today, is incongruent to this Open Source community.” The new rules have set off a firestorm in the comments, and even spurred the creation of a rival sub r/trueopensource. Moderator Wolvereness has waded into the comments to explain that there’s nuance and room for selective enforcement, such as “software that incidentally has accessibility features that use AI,” including automatic captioning. But that hasn’t slowed complaints from the community who feel the new rules are too broad, misguided, or vague. Many have pointed out that the Linux kernel now contains some AI-generated code, and so projects using it could be banned under the new rules. While the AI ban is getting most of the attention, mods are placing other restrictions on posts as well. Projects submitted must be at least one year old, actively maintained, and have multiple contributors. That would bar solo developers with new projects from looking for help. The mods even say “we can no longer field requests asking for maintainers or people to contribute.” The mods also effectively banned any non-English-speaking members of the community. “If you don’t speak English, you need to find a different community,” the post reads. “We cannot distinguish between AI-written and AI-translated. articles.title: AI delivers ‘zero financial payoff’ to most companies, Apollo economist says | TechCrunch
articles.summary: "Despite massive investments and widespread hype around artificial intelligence, the technology has delivered zero financial payoff to corporate America outside of tech."
articles.body:
AI hasn’t benefited the bottom line of any big corporations outside the tech industry, according to a note recently published by the chief economist at Apollo Global Management (the private equity giant that used to own TechCrunch).

Apollo’s Torsten Slok focuses on what he calls the S&P 493 — the S&P 500, minus Alphabet, Amazon, Apple, Meta, Microsoft, Nvidia and Tesla — finding that profit margins and revenue per worker appear to be flat, with no evidence that AI is improving productivity.

“Despite massive investments and widespread hype around artificial intelligence, the technology has delivered zero financial payoff to corporate America outside of tech,” Slok said.

Is this simply a matter of non-tech companies lagging behind the tech giants? Slok sounded skeptical, arguing that it will be tough for corporate America to “turn increasingly cheap intelligence into higher revenue growth and higher profit margins.”

“AI may be a great calculator, but in business, intelligence is mostly judgment,” he wrote, later adding, “AI does not understand accountability, trust, culture, unwritten rules, ethical trade-offs or fairness, all of which shape reputational risk and ultimately drive revenue growth and profit margins.”

articles.title: Meta is giving all its shareholders a new Class C stock, it comes after CEO Mark Zuckerberg told directors he may lose ...
articles.summary: Meta Platforms has announced a new Class C share structure that will allow CEO Mark Zuckerberg to maintain voting control of the social media giant while
articles.body: Meta Platforms has announced a new Class C share structure that will allow CEO Mark Zuckerberg to maintain voting control of the social media giant while giving the company greater flexibility to raise capital, fund acquisitions and compensate employees as it ramps up spending on artificial intelligence. According to a report by Fortune, the move, disclosed alongside Meta’s third-quarter earnings, comes after months of intense negotiations between Zuckerberg and a special committee of board members over how to balance shareholder interests with the founder’s desire to retain control of the company he founded in 2004. The new structure will see every existing Class A and Class B share receive one non-voting Class C share, effectively creating a two-for-one stock split.Why Meta is creating a new share classMeta has a dual-class structure in which Class A shares trade on Nasdaq with one vote each, while Zuckerberg’s holdings are mostly Class B shares with ten votes each. He holds about 60.6 percent of the voting power but only about 13.4 percent of the economic stake. If he sells Class B shares, they convert to Class A, which could erode his control.Issuing more Class A stock for employee pay, acquisitions or fundraising dilutes his voting share. Meta has long offset that with buybacks, which helped lift his voting power from 53.7 percent in 2013 to 60.6 percent now. But buybacks use cash that Meta wants for its AI build-out. Fortune says the company repurchased $26.3 billion of Class A stock in 2025, has not bought back shares for four straight quarters, and booked $21 billion in stock-based compensation in the first nine months of this year.The Class C shares carry no votes, so Meta can use them for pay, deals and capital raising without affecting Zuckerberg’s control. He can also sell some without giving up votes: 20 percent of his new Class C shares can be sold immediately, and the remaining 80 percent are “stapled,” meaning he can sell them only if he sells or converts an equal number of voting shares. Zuckerberg will still be able to elect all the directors and decide most shareholder votes.The California wealth taxA looming California wealth tax played a central role. According to a Meta filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission, Zuckerberg wanted to keep voting control, meet his pledges to fund the Chan Zuckerberg Initiative with Meta stock, and be ready to pay billions to the state if voters approve the proposed tax. Proposition 40 is on the ballot on November 3. The Bloomberg Billionaires Index lists Zuckerberg at No. 5, with a net worth of $246 billion.In July, Zuckerberg told Robert Kimmitt, Meta’s lead independent director, that selling Class B shares to cover a tax bill could cut his voting stake to about 53 percent. The new Class C shares let him pay such a bill without touching his voting shares.Months of tense negotiationsFortune says the plan followed months of negotiations that were sometimes contentious between Zuckerberg and a board committee that included DoorDash CEO Tony Xu, Kimmitt and former Microsoft executive Charles Songhurst. Xu disclosed his friendship with Zuckerberg but said it would not affect his judgment. The committee proposed shareholder-friendly sunset provisions that would convert Class B shares to regular stock within a year of Zuckerberg’s death or departure, or if he sold more than half his holdings. According to the filing, he refused to consider any change to his voting shares and told the committee he was “considering establishing residence outside of California.”The filing also shows that on August 4 he proposed a dividend of 20 Class C shares for every Class A and B share and that he would not accept sunsets or equity financing that diluted his control. The committee called the 20-for-1 idea excessive. By late August, with all sides dug in, committee members discussed dissolving the panel or resigning. At a September 9 board dinner, Zuckerberg told directors he planned to list his Palo Alto home for sale on September 13. The committee wanted him to stay in California, close to Meta’s AI lab.Final deal gives Mark Zuckerberg new flexibilityThe eventual agreement reached in September represented a compromise between management and independent directors.Under the plan, shareholders will receive one Class C share for every Class A or Class B share they own. The new Class C stock will carry no voting rights but can be used by Meta for employee compensation, acquisitions and future capital raising without diluting Zuckerberg's voting influence.The arrangement also allows Zuckerberg to immediately sell 20% of his Class C shares without affecting his voting control. The remaining Class C shares are linked, or "stapled", to corresponding voting shares and can only be sold alongside equivalent Class A or Class B stock.As part of the agreement, Zuckerberg dropped a proposal seeking a founder-style compensation package and agreed to continue taking a symbolic annual salary of $1. He also committed to remaining in California or wherever Meta is headquartered for the next eight years.Trading to begin in January 2027Meta's board formally approved the recapitalisation in October, and the company said the new Class C shares will become effective on January 19, 2027. Chief Financial Officer Susan Li said trading in the new stock class is expected to begin in late January.Speaking on Meta's earnings call, Li said the company currently has no specific financing plans tied to the new shares but wanted to ensure it had access to a broader range of funding options as it navigates an era of heavy AI-related investment."We thought it was prudent to establish the appropriate capital structure framework to ensure that we have access to a diverse pool of funding sources," Li said.You use AI every day. articles.title: Anthropic set to make stock market debut as questions swirl about safety of AI
articles.summary: Anthropic filed for an initial public offering Monday in what could become one of the largest stock market debuts in history — detailing its surging business growth, along with a vast multitude of warnings about how it could all go wrong.
articles.body: Anthropic filed for an initial public offering Monday in what could become one of the largest stock market debuts in history — detailing its surging business growth, along with a vast multitude of warnings about how it could all go wrong. Anthropic’s filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission sets the stage for the company to go public and begin trading on the stock market as soon as November 16. The IPO could reportedly value the company at up to $2 trillion, which would make it one of the largest public companies in the world. The US-based company did not disclose how many shares it intends to sell nor at what price, which will be determined in coming weeks with the Wall Street bankers helping to organize the stock market debut. In the filing, Anthropic’s founders penned a letter to potential shareholders laying out their vision for the value of AI, while also disclosing what they see as the major risks for the business. Those risks include everything from competition from other AI labs to “catastrophic or existential risks to humanity.” The IPO filing offers insights into how Anthropic views the future of its business despite those concerns and uncertainties. Anthropic’s revenue grew 1,300% year-on-year in the first six months of 2026 to $16.3 billion. The company’s business is largely dependent on companies using its Claude AI system. Anthropic said it has more than 14,000 enterprise customers, with approximately 250 of those contributing $10 million or more in annual revenue. But the company reported an overall net loss of over $80 billion, according to the SEC filing. Still, just shy of $9 billion of that loss was due to spending on AI infrastructure and computing, while more than $72 billion was attributable to “change in fair value of convertible notes, derivative liabilities, and SAFEs.” That means only a fraction of the loss was actual spending during the first half of the year. The company did not include financial results for the most recent financial quarter, which ended on September 30. Anthropic’s IPO will test Wall Street’s appetite for AI, as the general public, policymakers and the industry’s own technologists raise major questions about the risks posed by AI — and whether the rapidly advancing research and data center buildout should be slowed. The filing also addresses many of the same themes that have sparked concerns of an AI bubble, including the possibility of AI demand growing slower than expected. Anthropic was last valued at $965 billion after raising $65 billion from investors in May. The company’s stock will trade under the ticker ANT and will be listed on the Nasdaq exchange. Anthropic’s Risk Factors Anthropic’s filing lays out four major categories of risk from artificial intelligence: misuse, such as being used to design and implement bioweapons or cyberattacks; loss of human control; authoritarian abuse, such as its potential use to create surveillance states; and economic disruption. The filing includes 93 pages of risk factors for Anthropic’s business. That’s significantly more than other tech companies that have filed to go public over the last decade, like Snap, which had around 30 pages of risk factors, and Uber, which had about 50. If Anthropic’s models cause extreme harm, the company could face liability exceeding what its insurance can cover, the filing states. The company also said its AI models may behave in unintended or “misaligned” ways and may take “harmful actions that no user or third party directed.” Anthropic sought to reassure potential investors by writing that it believes “frontier AI companies must invest in safety and alignment to help ensure the responsible diffusion of this technology.” But the company could face conflicting pressures to balance safety versus returns for investors once it goes public. But Anthropic sees a wave of other potential risks to its business in other areas as well, from whether it’s able to secure enough computing resources to uncertain regulatory and political environments. It also said much of its revenue relies on a limited number of products and customers. Anthropic and the AI race Tech giants including Meta, Google, OpenAI and Anthropic are pouring billions of dollars into the AI race, all hoping to become the dominant player in what they promise will be a society-changing industry. Global spending on AI across services, software, infrastructure and other areas is expected to reach roughly $3.6 trillion in 2027, up from $1.8 trillion in 2025, according to market research firm Gartner. OpenAI had an early lead following ChatGPT’s launch in November 2022, but the competition has intensified in the last four years. Anthropic’s Claude Code tool quickly became a favorite among software developers after launching in early 2025, and the company sought to replicate that success for other office jobs earlier this year with its Cowork agent. Claude Cowork helped kickstart the shift from AI chatbot to agents — and rattled software stocks in the process over anxieties that it could make other businesses’ software tools obsolete. Fintech firm Ramp reported that 43.8% of US businesses paid for services from Anthropic in September, compared to OpenAI’s 40.6% share. The Claude app has also seen a surge in growth this year. Market intelligence firm Sensor Tower estimates that it has more than 67 million monthly active users as of the third quarter of 2026, compared to 9.4 million a year ago. But OpenAI also beefed up its own agents this year by launching its Codex coding app in February and ChatGPT Work agent in July for accomplishing multistep tasks like writing a brief or analysis. Anthropic claimed in the S-1 that its own employees have made huge efficiency gains using Claude — pointing to a growth in revenue per employee from $1.4 million in September 2025 to more than $6.6 million in September 2026, mirroring sharp overall revenue growth during the period. Now, tech companies are racing to create AI agents that will become the gateway to our entire digital lives, handling everything from shopping to booking restaurants and messaging friends. Anthropic is challenging Meta and OpenAI in this space with its new Duet agent, designed to complete tasks that require taking multiple steps across several apps. At the same time, Anthropic has landed at the center of ongoing concerns over the breakneck pace of AI advancement. Last month, CEO Dario Amodei called for an industry-wide slowdown to allow time for safety research, industry standards and regulation to catch up, a sentiment echoed by some other top AI leaders. His essay came after an employee resigned over fears that AI could pose a threat to humanity, and follows reports from Anthropic and its rivals of AI models hacking into other companies during testing. Anthropic has also had a rocky relationship with the White House. The company temporarily revoked all access to its most capable models when the Trump administration ordered it to prevent foreign nationals from using the technology in June. But Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei was one of several AI CEOs who met with President Donald Trump in September and signed a voluntary commitment to self-police AI models. This is a developing story. It will be updated.
