articles.title: Can AI help solve the COBOL code crisis?
articles.summary: The ancient code holding the world together may meet its match in AI. Today is not that day.
articles.body: What do the IRS, banks, airlines, and government infrastructure around the world have in common? They’re all running on systems propped up by antique computer code that nobody dares touch, lest everything come crashing down. OpenAI thinks it may have a solution. On October 19th, the company touted “substantial improvements” in its latest AI models’ ability to migrate aging software written in older programming languages into modern code, which it claims could help organizations with “maintaining and modernizing older systems.” That’s a potentially massive deal. COBOL, one of the languages highlighted by OpenAI, remains stubbornly embedded in vast portions of the world’s critical infrastructure. And despite decades of efforts to banish it to history, the language has limped on, simply refusing to die. It is hard to overstate COBOL’s ubiquity. Short for “common business-oriented language,” COBOL came into being in 1959. Nearly seven decades later, it is still everywhere. According to IBM, COBOL is the foundation for more than 40 percent of online banking systems, supports 80 percent of in-person credit card transactions, and handles 95 percent of ATM transactions. It also underpins many government systems, from Social Security to the IRS to services run by most states. One rough estimate puts the annual cost of COBOL’s inefficiencies to the US GDP at around $105 billion. But replacing COBOL is fiendishly difficult. The same goes for other legacy programming languages, like Fortran, still in use today for everything from scientific computing and weather forecasting to atmospheric and ocean studies and codes critical to nuclear security. These systems are often too important to risk breaking, and many of the programmers who understand them have long since retired or died. For all their impressive advances in modern software development, AI coding tools have struggled to make much headway with these legacy systems. But recent developments suggest that may be changing. In its latest blog post, OpenAI reported promising results migrating COBOL code to more modern programming languages, including C++, Java, Kotlin, Python, and Rust, without changing what the original software does. That last bit is crucial for organizations looking to ditch code like COBOL, and OpenAI acknowledges that “a migration is considered successful only if all tests pass.” In OpenAI’s own tests, GPT-6.1 Sol achieved 87 percent behavior preservation accuracy at low reasoning effort — how many computational steps the model spends analyzing a problem before giving an answer — climbing to 98 percent at higher reasoning. By comparison, at low reasoning effort, GPT-6 Astra scored around 86 percent, GPT-6 Sol just 21 percent, and GPT-5.6 Sol a mere 5 percent. “These evaluation results demonstrate progress toward more accurate, affordable code migration for teams modernizing the software their businesses depend on,” OpenAI wrote. The company also reported improvements on its models’ ability to build database software in various programming languages, including COBOL. Anthropic also sees an opportunity in legacy systems. In February, it published a step-by-step “code modernization playbook” and pitched its coding agent, Claude Code, as a way to migrate COBOL code into modern languages like Java or Python. It offered no performance benchmarks showing how well Claude Code could perform such migrations, but declared that “the economics of COBOL modernization have shifted.” Shares in IBM, which derives part of its revenue helping companies maintain legacy systems, nosedived following Anthropic’s announcement. Experts who spoke to The Verge agreed that AI tools have made strides in tackling legacy code in recent years. But they cautioned that advances trumpeted by OpenAI this week are a very long way from making it possible to safely replace critical legacy systems built around it. OpenAI spokesperson Oscar Haines acknowledged in an email to The Verge that legacy code “is still far from a solved problem” and said the company is listening to feedback from developers and enterprises and exploring ways to build better tests and continue improving its models’ understanding of coding languages. Anthropic did not provide comment in time for publication. “Rewriting code is not the same as replacing a system,” said Vadim Zaytsev, an associate professor of software evolution at the University of Twente in the Netherlands. Systems do have a lot of code — Zaytsev said the largest system he’d seen had 250 million lines of COBOL, “definitely not the world’s largest” — but that’s only part of the problem. Code may be written in multiple languages and there’s data, potentially stored in various formats, to consider, he said. There are also technical integrations with other systems and the expectations of the people and organizations to bear in mind. All that complexity means “AI is not playing a major role at the moment in replacing or migrating legacy COBOL systems,” Zaytsev said. OpenAI’s evaluations don’t capture this complex reality either, Arie van Deursen, a software engineering professor at Delft University of Technology in the Netherlands, told The Verge. He described the company’s blog as “superficial,” noting it offered few details about the migration task, while its language benchmark tested models on a relatively simple and well-defined task involving systems similar to those they would have encountered in training. He also stressed the huge gap between maintaining an aging system and modernizing it. “Maintaining is of course a lot easier than modernizing,” van Deursen said, calling the tasks OpenAI used to assess its models “lightyears” away from actual modernization. “The evaluations shown by OpenAI don’t address the key difficulty: Breaking up a complex legacy system into smaller units that can be replaced individually.” The biggest challenge isn’t necessarily rewriting code. “The main challenge is indeed not understanding how the system works,” said Alastair Donaldson, a professor of programming languages at Imperial College London. Such a lack of understanding is a “very common” problem for legacy systems using languages like COBOL, he said, adding that very few people know how to program in them anymore. And while it is everywhere, Donaldson said “nobody in their right mind would use COBOL for a new development project.” That makes robust testing crucial, Donaldson said. One approach could be to run the same workflows through the old and new systems to check they behave identically. AI could also document its code translation, ideally allowing humans familiar with the legacy language to review the work. Formal verification, which uses mathematical techniques to computationally verify that code behaves correctly, is another option, said Jacopo Mauro, a mathematics and computer science professor at the University of Southern Denmark. Such methods are already used to verify AI-generated mathematical results, but applying them to legacy code would require a “huge amount of work,” Mauro said. Using those methods would mean code could be checked automatically, Mauro said, adding that “having this will be better than having a human check that the translation is correct.” Until then, he said, “human verification remains essential.” And when the systems involved are as critical as those running on COBOL, experts say you need to be absolutely certain the replacement works. “In many cases even minor differences in system behaviour before and after migration are unacceptable,” Zaytsev said. While AI can definitely deliver savings and speed things up, the complexity of legacy systems means partial automation isn’t enough. “Suppose you have a magic AI wand that handles 99 percent of your code,” Zaytsev said. “What do you do with the remaining 1 percent? That 1 percent can be a million lines of code, spread all over the place and subtly failing in more ways you can imagine within your lifetime.”

articles.title: Anthropic warns of AI's 'catastrophic risks' ahead of blockbuster share listing
articles.summary: The company will be the first true artificial intelligence company to go public as tech firms continue to invest heavily in AI.
articles.body:
Anthropic has warned artificial intelligence could pose "catastrophic or existential risks to humanity" as it unveiled details of its planned blockbuster stock market listing in the US.

The company behind AI chatbot Claude revealed losses of more than $80.7bn (£60.5bn) in the first half of the year, but said it had $112.4bn in cash or equivalents, and generated revenues of $16.3bn over the same period.

The number of shares to be released, their price range, and a date for the listing have not been disclosed.

Anthropic's valuation when it goes public has been expected to exceed that of SpaceX, which this summer was the biggest-ever stock listing at an initial valuation of about $1.8 trillion.

In a filing ahead of its listing, Anthropic said concerns had been raised by policymakers, regulators and researchers as well as by people within its organisation that AI systems posed a significant risk to humanity.

It said advanced AI systems "could, if not developed, deployed, and operated with appropriate safeguards, oversight, and security measures, pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity, particularly if such systems were misused, replicated, weaponised, or allowed to operate with a high degree of autonomy".

Anthropic will be the first true AI company to go public, making it a test case for the future of the technology.

It said it will list on the Nasdaq under the symbol ANT.

Anthropic, which was founded just five years ago by chief executive Dario Amodei, his sister Daniela Amodei and five other co-founders, announced its intention to go public in June.

Its most significant rival, OpenAI, quickly followed suit, saying it, too, intended to go public. That listing is now expected to occur early next year, according to a person familiar with OpenAI's plans.

After the companies had decided on such plans, a wave of cyber-security and other types of technological breaches occurred involving their AI agents, or AI bots that are designed to operate somewhat autonomously.

Current and former staff of both companies also gained public attention with new warnings that AI technology was being developed without the ability to protect the whole of humanity from possible future harms enacted by AI tools.

In Anthropic's new documents, it reiterated promises it has made in the past to develop AI in a way that is beneficial to people, while at the same time warning investors of its dangers.

In its financial filings, Anthropic detailed losses that exceeded its revenue for the first half of the year, but said it would often make forward investments "that may seem irresponsibly large at first glance".

"In general, we will aim to be bold but sane, and to win trust with a track record of successful bets," the tech giant said.

Its success depends largely on its ability to develop the most advanced AI models, Anthropic said, adding, "any failure to do so could adversely affect our business".

Tech companies have been heavily investing in costly AI infrastructure and tools, like data centres and the informational models that underly all AI technology, pouring more than $1tn into the efforts over the last year alone.

Why are there concerns AI could threaten humanity, and how real are they?

articles.title: Anthropic’s IPO filing lays out a plan to ‘revolutionize every area of human endeavor’ with AI
articles.summary: Anthropic’s public S-1 filing ahead of its planned blockbuster IPO is now available, revealing more details about the AI lab behind Claude.
articles.body: Anthropic has filed its S-1 prospectus with the Securities and Exchange Commission, preparing the company behind Claude to beat OpenAI to the punch with an IPO. In a filing with the SEC, Anthropic said it plans to list on the Nasdaq exchange under the ticker symbol “ANT.” The AI company confidentially filed with the SEC earlier this year in June, but the public document reveals more details, as well as the company’s plans for the future in its own words, as well as potential risks for investors and the world. According to the S-1, in the first half of this year Anthropic had an $80.7 billion net loss on $16.3 billion in revenue. As previously reported by the Wall Street Journal based on leaked versions of the document, the majority of that loss is from accounting charges related to notes issued by the company for funding. It also lays out billions of dollars in deals it’s made for access to compute to power its AI, including about $3.1 billion per month to SpaceX for access to Nvidia GPUs once all of the planned capacity is delivered, totaling as much as $120.5 billion by 2029. Other commitments include spending $44.9 billion with Microsoft through 2033, at least $114.5 billion with Google through 2033, and $110 billion with Amazon over the next ten years. > Anthropic: > We believe that AI is one of the most consequential technologies in human history. If managed well, it could rapidly accelerate scientific innovation, greatly increase economic growth rates, bring cures for major diseases within reach, and solve problems that have resisted generations of human effort. > Anthropic aims to realize these benefits while navigating and preventing the risks that come with a technological revolution this fast and this powerful. There are four things that we would like any investor in Anthropic to understand: the incredible potential of AI, the risks we must address, Anthropic’s unique approach to building a company and operating in the world, and the ways in which our behavior may differ from that of a purely profit-maximizing company. According to the filing, cofounder and chief executive officer Dario Amodei’s compensation totaled nearly $18 million in 2025, most of which came from stock and option awards. His sister, Daniela Amodei, who also cofounded the company and serves as its president and director, was the second highest-paid executive, receiving $16.4 million in 2025. Anthropic set out a long list of risk factors that could affect its business, including the prospect of its AI models developing “forms of sentience,” “AI-specific taxes,” and unfavorable resolutions to the many ongoing copyright disputes relating to how its models are trained. The company also warned about the risk of “catastrophic” AI-related incidents, and said it was likely no single insurer — “and potentially the insurance industry in the aggregate” — could underwrite such risk. This is a developing story...

articles.title: Kevin Roose is AGI-pilled. Why aren’t you?
articles.summary: The former New York Times journalist on cofounding Machine Gods, chronicling the AGI race, and why he believes the singularity is near.
articles.body: Today, I’m talking to Kevin Roose, journalist and author of the new book The AGI Chronicles, which details the recent and explosive transformation of the AI industry. Kevin was a longtime New York Times reporter and host of the popular podcast Hard Fork, but he and friend of the show Casey Newton just left the Times to start the all-new tech podcast Machine Gods, which launched last week. Kevin and I talked about launching Machine Gods and what it’s like to go from The New York Times to being an independent creator — and then of course we talked about the book, which is an excellently reported dive into the companies racing to build artificial general intelligence. I wanted to get a sense from Kevin of what it was like to report this, to try and understand these characters and this moment in time, and where it all goes next. Fair warning: This conversation takes a pretty philosophical turn at the end, but I think you’ll find it a really worthwhile back-and-forth. Okay: Kevin Roose on The AGI Chronicles, starting Machine Gods, and where AI goes from here. Here we go. This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity. Kevin Roose, you are the author of The AGI Chronicles and the cofounder and co-host of the new podcast Machine Gods. Welcome to Decoder. Thanks so much for having me. I was listening to the first episode of Machine Gods and you and Casey discussed the fact that technically you have the title of CEO. It’s true. I won the coin flip and we needed someone. When you start a company as we have, you need to list someone as the CEO, I guess, to know who to haul in front of Congress when our first scandal inevitably breaks. So that’s going to be me. It’s funny because you’re a CEO on Decoder. It means I’m going to have to ask you the Decoder questions. [Laughs] Okay. Well, I’ve been a CEO for about five minutes and most days I frankly forget I’m the CEO. Honestly, that tracks with most of the CEOs on the show. They all act like they’ve only done it for five minutes. We’ll come to it. I want to talk about your book. It’s called The AGI Chronicles. It is a meticulously reported book about the main frontier labs and the culture shift they’ve all undergone as AI has come into the forefront and become a much more commercial product in many ways. But let’s just start with Machine Gods. You were a journalist for The New York Times for a long time. Obviously, I think the audience probably knows this, but you and I have known each other for a long time. I will say that since I have known you, your desire to be a YouTuber has been top of mind. You’re just like, “How do I get over there?” And I’ve always been like, “Run, don’t do it.” But you did it. You left The Times, you started your own podcast with our friend Casey Newton. It is the next generation of the very popular podcast, Hard Fork, which was excellent. And I’m excited for you, but what made you take the leap? --- [Image: Verge subscribers, don’t forget you get exclusive access to ad-free Decoder wherever you get your podcasts. Head here. Not a subscriber? You can sign up here. --- Yeah, you have been trying to convince me out of this for as long as I’ve been trying to convince myself into it and you have not succeeded because here I am. Yep, I failed. Utterly failed. No, look, I think that for some very good reasons, media companies have long been a little bit wary of going all in on YouTube or any other video platform. The ones that have gone all in have not necessarily come out of that with good feelings about it because there are a lot of– Yeah, they pivot to video and also into death, routinely. Yeah, you pivot to video or you sort of waste a bunch of money doing things that don’t pay for themselves. So, I think there are some structural economic reasons for that, but I also think it’s that there aren’t a lot of institutions that are equipped to make that kind of a long-term bet. I’ve been trying to YouTube-pill people in media for many years, as you know. You’ve been trying to undo the YouTube-pilling on your end, but I just think it’s clearly the most important media platform in the world right now. It’s a place where journalism has not historically had a central place. If you were to look at YouTube as a whole and try to assess what piece of it is dedicated to what you or I would consider high-quality journalism, it’s a vanishingly small part of the overall ecosystem there. So, part of my mission is just to crack that and figure out how to do YouTube and video in general in a way that is sustainable from an economic and a sort of creative standpoint. And then just to experiment and do a bunch of things. This is not a face that needs to be on YouTube. So I’m also hoping to bring some other people in and nail some formats. But I look at what The Verge has done there. I look at what people like Joanna Stern and MKBHD have done there. To me, that is very exciting and it’s a space where there’s a lot less competition than text or podcasts. Machine Gods is a podcast that you’re doing in partnership with NPR, which I want to talk about. But do you think of it as a YouTube product? We want it to be video-first. What that means basically is that we are going to give a shit about what it looks like to a degree that we have not always done. We’re going to try to give people a lot of reasons to want to watch as well as listen. Obviously, we know that there are some people who just don’t like video podcasts and so we want to give the audio audience something that is enjoyable, but this is the direction of things. You can’t do a podcast now without doing video on top of it. So we’re going to try to really embrace that and make a good version of it that is as good as two middle-aged journalists can pull off on YouTube. Truly the future of media is middle-aged journalists pivoting to YouTube. I feel the same way because I’m now making more video and that’s what we’re doing. It’s going to be great. The other reason to leave and to do this — and obviously people know I’m friends with Casey as well, and I’ve been talking to you and him about it for a long time — is that the AI story is here. There is a platform shift. There are new companies, new characters, new ideas to talk about in the world. It’s funny because in that context, usually you get a media shift as well. The way we tell stories or the formats we tell stories usually shifts alongside the thing we are talking about or the technology we’re talking about. Here, YouTube feels like the most solid media foundation that exists. It’s the one that’s the same the most, even though it’s changing and it has YouTube Shorts and now you can A/B test everything, including your own face. But it’s the one that is the most the same. Instagram has undergone some massive change and it feels like that will continue happening. Does it feel like YouTube is the most stable place to build as you’re trying to tell these new stories? It does. I mean, obviously you never want to put all your eggs in one basket. So, we are also distributing video on Apple Podcasts and Spotify and we’re going to be everywhere. But yeah, it feels relatively stable. The question I’m always wondering is what would it take to replace YouTube? Many companies have tried to replace YouTube, but to do that, you would not only have to build an experience that was better for creators and better for users, but you would also have to replicate the entire visual corpus of humanity. You would have to just get six million videos from plumbers about how to fix every individual sink and then upload it to that. It’s a really hard thing to displace. It is so ingrained for so many people, and I just think it’s going to keep growing. We’ll come to this when we talk about AI, but a long time ago I asked Google CEO Sundar Pichai, “Well, what are you going to do if there’s no more websites?” And he was kind of like, “Well, we have YouTube.” And there’s just no arguing with that. You sure do. And it is just going to keep growing. What has been the most surprising thing about going from The New York Times to what you might call the creator economy? Well, we’re very new at it, but surprising to me so far is how much I like all the business stuff. I think in journalism, you’re always taught to stay in your lane, and I have never run a business before. Casey has run a business. I knew he enjoyed it. But for me, these are new muscles and I don’t enjoy all of it. Negotiating the insurance quotes for our defamation coverage is not what I would feel compelled by. But regarding actually running a business, there is something to this founder thing. Yeah, it’s a good time. It’s funny, in talking to you and to Casey and Joanna, who also just left and started her own thing, that comes up a lot. From my perspective, it’s why I’ve been doing this a long time. What if I stopped running the business? That doesn’t seem to be a choice. This is the future of media — taking control of your business and taking control of your audience. There’s something very powerful there. One of the things I want to talk about, and then I definitely want to talk about the book at length, is the audience for AI coverage, because I see it in two ways. There’s a group of people building the stuff that loves it and wants to consume all of it. There’s a group of people that truly hates it and thinks all of it is fake. And then there’s what I would call an expanding group in the middle where the products have become more useful. You have to look at them and evaluate them as they are. They were not terribly useful a couple years ago. The promises did not match reality, but every day now it can do one more thing that it couldn’t do before. Whether that thing is hacking all of the websites in the world, we’ll set that aside, but AI can do things it couldn’t do before and the audience seems to be changing. How are you thinking about the audience for Machine Gods and how it might grow or change? I mean, right now we’re just trying a bunch of stuff that we think will be good and we hope that it will find its sort of natural audience. But I think you’re right that the audience is changing. I think for a while there was a lot of demand for cope — basically people telling you this is not happening, you don’t have to pay attention to it, it sucks, it’s hurting the environment. There still is in some parts of the internet. YouTube has a weird amount of this still going on and Reddit is also very anti-AI. But I think most people, or at least maybe a plurality of people, are either resigned to or excited about the fact that this is not going away. That is the audience that we’re looking for. We’re not trying to tell you that AI is amazing and we’re going to be in AI utopia under the new machine regime. We’re also not telling you that this stuff is fake and sucks and is going to go away on its own and so we don’t need to do anything to regulate it or be worried about it. Casey’s phrase for this is AI realism. He thinks there’s a big chunk of people who are just sort of curious and interested and maybe a little scared, but their reaction to the fear is not to try to bury their heads in the sand, but to try to understand the thing. So we started feeling this when we were doing Hard Fork where we would do something that just seemed kind of not our vibe. We would do a Claude Code walkthrough tutorial where we would just spend half an hour building a website and film ourselves and throw it up and it would do great. So people clearly were curious, and even if the comments on the videos were all from people who hated AI, there was clearly a lot of demand out there for people who were just like, “I kind of want to know what’s going on.” “I hate that I can’t stop watching this” is a real theme inside of AI coverage for a variety of reasons. Let’s talk about the book. I think that’s going to frame a bunch of the other questions I have. The book is meticulously reported. It is really fun to read. And the point of it, as I’ve heard you describe it, is to tell the history of the deep learning revolution because all these people just talk in Signal and in extremely childish tweets. Tell me about that gap because this is an industry that is obsessed with documenting itself for computers and being legible to computers and not at all to other people, which seems wild to me. So explain the reporting of this book, because it feels like convincing them to even tell you what happened was a slog. It was, yeah. So basically the reason I wrote this is because I was scared that all of this stuff was going to disappear. I am a history buff. I love to read books about the Wright brothers or the electrification of rural America or the moments of great invention during the PC revolution. I’m such a sucker for that stuff. What you notice as you read more of these books is just that they all rely on a lot of contemporaneous notes and evidence — the lab notes from the scientists developing the atomic bomb, the correspondence between the Wright brothers and their friends and business partners — that is preserved and archived. It was just clear to me reporting on AI every day that there was not going to be anything remotely similar for this stuff because A, all the people building this stuff work for private companies. They’re not government employees who are legally required to preserve their correspondence. And B, the Signal messages and Slack messages are all set by the lawyers to auto-delete after a certain period. So there was literally going to be kind of a mass disappearance with each passing year of these, I think, historically important artifacts, moments, and stories. And then C, the researchers are all too busy to keep notes. They’re all grinding because they’re trying to build the machine god. So, I thought as a journalist, but more so almost as a historian, which is not a role I’ve ever officially played, but one I think I was playing with this book. I was just like, “I’ve got to just get this stuff because I have this sort of privileged ringside seat. These people talk to me. I know some of them will sit down and talk to me and tell me the stories.” We did a lot of it on background so they could be protected from the consequences of talking to me. But this was sort of my attempt to furiously get all the stuff and put it in the archive where future generations could look at it. The theme that really jumps out at me as I read the book was there’s a moment when AGI goes from being a thing they’re all dreaming about to being a thing that they all have to build and the shackles come off and they say, “We have to do this,” and they all drive toward it as hard as they can. You talk specifically about Google where the Overton window moved and suddenly the people inside of Google, who thought this was all a pipe dream and pretty silly, started talking about AGI. That moment feels like the single most important moment in the history of AI, where “Won’t it be great?” goes to “We better go as fast as we can.” Talk about that a little bit, because that shift inside these companies feels under-reported. Yeah, I think that’s absolutely right. I mean, people have been talking and writing about AGI or some precursor that wasn’t called AGI but meant the same thing since literally antiquity. And especially since the 1950s, when the term artificial intelligence was born, people were talking about it. Alan Turing was writing about the thinking machine that could do anything the human brain could. So this concept has been around for a long time, but there was no technology anywhere on the market or in research labs that could actually do what people wanted it to do — that could take in information, learn to learn about that information, and then use that to make predictions and act in the world. People tried lots of different ways to do this and none of them worked all that well. What really needed to happen was the transformer needed to come along. This architecture that Google developed in 2017 and published and then presented to, among other places, OpenAI, which took the idea of the transformer and ran with it. And that’s the T in ChatGPT today. But that was the– Somewhere a Google PR person just leapt out of a bush to hand you a check. They do love this line. They love it when you say it. They get so happy. They love it. They love it less when you point out that although they invented it, they absolutely failed to turn it into a product until after OpenAI did. But yeah, it was a dream, but there was nothing to attach to the dream. There was no technology. And then the large language model came and suddenly it was like, “Oh, maybe this is the thing that could scale forever and keep improving over many orders of magnitude.” So, that’s the light bulb that goes off at OpenAI and then later at Google is like, “Now we have the tool to do the thing that we have always wanted to do.” You’ve got a line in there where you just point out that next-token prediction has not failed yet — that it is doing all the things people want it to do. We’ve obviously had to develop lots of technology around it. There are harnesses to make agents work. There’s reinforcement learning. There’s all this stuff around it. But that core technology has scaled. The reason I bring that up is that in 2023 into 2024, I would ask every AI person who would come on the show or that we would see on The Verge whether LLMs can do it. Can they do the thing you want them to do? Because I don’t think at that moment it was clear that they could. We’re closer now. They’re all openly talking about AGI. We are watching Meta’s Muse just walk its little butt around the internet whenever it wants. Do you think LLMs can do it? Do you think they can get there? I think they can. I’m not certain about that, but they’ve been shockingly good and effective so far. If you go back and you look at the first LLMs, it’s just like 99 percent of people thought this is crazy, that this won’t scale. And then it just keeps working at every stage, at every order of magnitude. I’ve asked people, what was it about next-token prediction that was clearly superior to everything that came before it? There have been people who have told me this actually exists in the human brain too. There’s a whole school of thought that says that what is happening inside the human brain is essentially next-token prediction at scale. Obviously, it’s more complicated. These are not one-for-one replicas of each other. But I think this is the fundamental mystery at the heart of AI: why is next-token prediction so remarkably effective? I think we don’t know. I kind of think it’s one of these cosmic mysteries, but why all of this works is because next-token prediction turns out to generalize really, really, really well. There’s a part of that where all these companies had to believe it. Dario Amodei of Anthropic obviously wrote his paper, “Big Blob of Compute,” where he said you can just do it. You can just dump data and compute at this and we’ll get there. Everyone else had to be convinced of this. What path did the AI companies all take to be convinced of this, and are they all fully convinced of it now? I don’t think they’re all fully convinced of it now. I think they are convinced of it to varying degrees. Ilya Sutskever has this phrase, “Feel the AGI,” that he would walk floor to floor at OpenAI chanting in the old days and reminding people to feel the AGI. I think the labs feel the AGI to varying degrees. I think Anthropic is clearly the most AGI-pilled of the labs, with OpenAI kind of a close second. And then there’s Google, which I think has always struggled to feel the AGI. I think there are lots of reasons for that, but it’s very funny. I love this section of the book where there’s this internal memo battle at Google, where they would just go on their internal message boards and Googlers love to write these manifestos and then snipe at each other’s manifestos and things like that. So a researcher writes this memo, “Say AGI,” which is all about how Google — if it wants to win in AI, recruit the top technical talent, and remain safe about how it’s developing AI — has to admit, through using this term AGI, that what they are building is more than just a bunch of tools to make your Gmail better and make your docs better and make your Google Photos better at recognizing the people’s faces. It is all actually building up to something like a kind of human-level general intelligence. And then someone else immediately writes a memo that’s like, “Don’t say AGI, it’s a horrible, unscientific term.” They go back and forth like this for a while, and you’ll notice even today, [Google CEO] Sundar Pichai does not say AGI. No, he won’t. Demis Hassabis says AGI. Sergey Brin says AGI. So I think there are kind of factions within Google that either think this is still crazy and we should talk about these things as narrow tools versus I think this growing and ascendant faction that is saying, “No, no, no, we’re building AGI, or at least we better say we’re building AGI because otherwise all of our top people are going to go work for OpenAI or Anthropic.” I think you and I had the same experience at Google I/O in May, where we watched Demis Hassabis end the whole keynote by saying, “We’re in the foothills of the singularity.” And then we both went and interviewed Sundar and said, “What does that mean?” And he was like, “Yeah, yeah, Demis. Cool guy.” [Laughs] Take it up with Demis. He was like, “What a kooky character that guy is, building the machine god over here. Let me tell you about the new features in Google Assistant.” There’s some big disconnect there that maybe explains everything about Google at this point in time. The reason I’m asking about this in particular, about this moment when they all clicked over to realize somehow we have to talk about it, is that OpenAI and Anthropic were founded to do this. They were built to make this happen. But they don’t agree on how it should work. I saw you at your book party in New York and you said that you could have retitled your book “Fuck That Guy,” because they all truly hate each other. It’s true. And yet it seems like they have the exact same idea — that they can get there with this technology. The commercial imperatives on OpenAI and Anthropic are very different from the commercial imperatives for Google. Right now, as you and I are talking, it’s not clear to me that they can get to AGI before they run out of money or before CoreWeave collapses or before the bubble writ large comes to some other conclusion about the state of the economy. Do you think that their religious fervor at AGI is keeping them from running a business? If I ran Anthropic today, a logical thing you could say is we should stop training new models and sell the very capable ones we have to more people. I think that belief in AGI is a double-edged sword. I think on one level, yes, if you are super AGI-pilled as the CEO of a frontier AI company, you are going to struggle to care about things like what is my profit margin on inference? Where is my next slate of enterprise customers coming from? Because how boring is that compared to “we are going to build the superhuman machine intelligence that leads us into the post-singularity future”? On the other hand, I think belief is actually a key ingredient in AI success, because belief and the ability to act on that belief is what leads you to do these bet-the-farm moves that can really pay off and have really paid off. Do you remember a year ago when everyone was saying, “Oh my God, OpenAI is spending so much money on compute; how are they ever going to pay for all this compute? Isn’t Sam Altman overextending?” Even Dario was giving interviews where he was throwing shade at OpenAI for spending so much goddamn money on compute. Fast-forward a year and OpenAI is now the only major AI company that is not severely compute-constrained. That belief that led Sam and his executives to bet and maybe overbet on compute last year was the reason that they are in a better position than Google or Anthropic or Meta or anyone else today. So I don’t want to say it’s always a liability to believe this hard, because I think it actually does allow you to make the bets that do end up paying off if the scaling continues to work. It’s interesting because I might reframe that OpenAI decision. You write very poignantly in your book about what people at OpenAI call “the blip,” where Sam Altman was fired for 20 minutes and then he came back and that cleared out a bunch of people from OpenAI. It is the moment you described in the book where OpenAI went from being a research company into being a business. The rational business decision was, “We need to sell more AI to people. We ought to have as much of it as we can.” And Sam is well known to be a ruthless business person. I’ve heard people describe him as S-tier at raising money, which is just an incredible Silicon Valley phrase. So I look at that as a business choice. They got rid of a bunch of stuff they were doing. They pivoted to making enterprise AI products, which is where the money is, and then they realized they needed to service that demand. You’re saying that was a bet on AGI, which to me is a more idealistic turn. Can you square those two? Yeah, I think it absolutely is a bet on AGI because Sora, which they launched and spent a bunch of money and compute on and then killed, is a cool toy that might open up a new line of business for you, but it is not going to get you closer to AGI. What actually gets you closer to AGI is sparking recursive self-improvement by building really good coding models and then turning them back on themselves. That was something that Anthropic was doing. OpenAI got distracted by the side quests and shiny objects that it had last year, and the company was getting its asses kicked. So OpenAI decided to trim the sails, cut fat, and really focus on coding and long-horizon agentic workloads. That is, as of now, the leading path to AGI or to whatever comes after AGI. So yes, I think that was absolutely a bet on conserving resources by not spending them on things like Sora, but what they did spend it on was trying to catch up with Anthropic in coding so that they could reach AGI. So when I look at Dario Amodei at Dreamforce standing next to Marc Benioff and he’s talking about selling enterprise software, is that just for show? That’s the thing I’m trying to square is they’ve all become enterprise software vendors in the realest way. They are B2B SaaS companies in the realest way now, but they’re also building God. You know these folks. Does that align? Are they like, “I have to take off my B2B SaaS hat now and go back to the altar?” I think the B2B SaaS thing is the game that they realize they have to play, but I don’t think it is any of their true passions. I was talking with Sam Altman for this book and one of the things he said was basically all of this was an accident: “I was never supposed to be running a giant tech company; that just didn’t factor in.” But now you wake up and you’ve got thousands of employees. Dario Amodei also has this very funny in retrospect document that he wrote in 2021 when they were just starting the company. It’s called “Vision for a NewCo.” You can go back and look at the predictions that Dario made about AGI, and one of them is he thinks that it will cost about $10 billion to build a full-fledged AGI, which was, I think, off by at least one order of magnitude and probably multiples. articles.title: Anthropic officially files for its public debut | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Anthropic has officially filed for an IPO, revealing soaring revenue, mounting losses, major enterprise adoption, and an unusual governance structure designed to preserve founder control and its AI safety mission.
articles.body:
After weeks of leaked S-1s , Anthropic finally filed for an initial public offering on Monday, setting the stage for one of the most closely watched public debuts in modern U.S. history.

Anthropic, which plans to list under the ticker “ANT,” recorded $16.3 billion for the first half of 2026, up from $1.2 billion in the same period last year, according to the firm’s latest SEC filing.

That revenue came off the back of an operating loss of $693 million, an improvement from the $2.1 billion in operating losses that Anthropic recorded in the first half of 2025. Anthropic’s net loss, however, hit $80.7 billion, which was largely driven by noncash accounting adjustments tied to convertible debt. The company says it “may not achieve or sustain profitability in the future.”

The filing also provided more color on the scale of Anthropic’s enterprise business. As of the end of September, Anthropic had more than 11,900 customers spending $100,000 or more annually; 1,900 customers spending $1 million or more; and about 250 customers spending $10 million or more.

As previously reported , Anthropic’s governance structure will enable Anthropic’s seven co-founders to maintain control once the company goes public. Dario Amodei, Daniela Amodei, Tom Brown, Jack Clark, Jared Kaplan, Sam McCandlish, and Chistopher Olah will make up the “Founder LLC,” which will collectively control 50.1% of shareholder voting power — a move Anthropic says is designed to preserve the company’s AI safety mission, per the filing.

Anthropic’s Long-Term Benefit Trust, established in 2023 to ensure the company pursues its public benefit mission , will have the authority to appoint most of the company’s board.

The governance structure is controversial because it means voting power is not proportional to the founders’ economic ownership, and therefore public shareholders will have little practical control over a company building technology that, by its own admission, poses “catastrophic or existential risks to humanity.”

Anthropic hasn’t yet disclosed how much it hopes to raise nor its proposed share price.
